title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-320-178-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-320-178-001
Stipulation
The parties agreed that Claimant earned an average weekly wage (AWW) of
$752.40.
Issues
1. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
sustained a compensable back injury during the course and scope of his employment
with Employer on June 12, 2025.
2. Whether Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence
that he is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical benefits that are causally
related to his June 12, 2025 industrial injury.
3. Whether the right to select the authorized treating physician (ATP) has
passed to Claimant.
4. Whether Claimant has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence
that he is entitled to temporary partial disability (TPD) benefits for the period July 15,
2025 until August 25, 2025.
5. Whether Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he
is entitled to temporary total disability (TTD) benefits for the period August 26, 2025 until
terminated by statute.
Findings of Fact
1. Employer is a family-owned Vietnamese restaurant. Claimant worked for
Employer as a cook and performed general cleaning functions. While working at the
restaurant on June 12, 2025 Claimant attempted to pick up a box of chicken from the
floor. He sought to place the box on a shelf in the walk-in cooler. Claimant was
attempting to perform the task quickly because he was also cooking chicken on the grill.
When picking up the box of chicken he felt a sharp pain in the right side of his lower
back. Claimant immediately reported the injury to his supervisor, Cipriano, but
completed his workday.

2. Claimant purchased naproxen after completing his work shift on June 12,
2025. He did not immediately seek professional medical treatment because he believed
the pain would resolve.
3. Claimant testified that a few days after June 12, 2025 he reported to
Employer’s owner Lien that he suffered a work injury. Lien did not provide Claimant with
a list of any medical providers. Notably, Claimant never received a list of medical
providers from Respondents.
4. Claimant remarked that he began working fewer hours for Employer due
to his back pain. He could not perform his job functions and stand on his feet for long
periods. Lien told Claimant she found someone else to replace him because he
frequently needed to leave work early or could not report to work because of his back
pain. Claimant did not return to work for Employer after August 21, 2025.
5. Employer records reveal Claimant continued to work after June 12, 2025
and earned $752.40 per week until July 14, 2025. Between July 14, 2025 and August
25, 2025 Claimant earned less than $752.40 each week. There are no documented
earnings after August 25, 2025.
6. The record reflects Claimant sought chiropractic treatment from Aim High
Health, LLC on August 18-19, 2025. He reported acute complaints in the lumbar, right
sacroiliac, right posterior pelvis/hip, right buttock, right posterior knee and right calf
“since 3 months ago.” Diagnoses included lumbar facet syndrome, lower back pain,
muscle spasm in the back, and pain in the right leg.
7. On August 22, 2025 Claimant sought emergency treatment from Denver
Health for “back pain” and “sciatica of the right side.” Providers prescribed medications
including cyclobenzaprine and naproxen. Claimant returned to Denver Health on
September 24, 2025 for “leg pain” and “right-sided sciatica.” Although providers ordered
an MRI of the lumbar spine, there is no evidence the diagnostic testing was performed.
8. On September 26, 2025 Claimant reported to the HCA HealthONE clinic
for right-sided lower back pain with right-sided sciatica. Travis Barlock, MD remarked he

was concerned Claimant had a herniated disc in the lower back. He recommended an
MRI and prescribed prednisone, naproxen, and gabapentin. Dr. Barlock also suggested
Claimant follow-up with Susan Nack, MD for his back pain.
9. On October 1, 2025 Claimant completed a Workers’ Claim for
Compensation. He recounted that on June 12, 2025 he was lifting a heavy box of
chicken at work and felt a pop in his back. Claimant noted pain in his lower back, right
leg and foot.
10. On October 1, 2025 Claimant visited physician’s assistant (PA) Jason
Bruno at CareNow Urgent Care for treatment. Claimant reported he had been suffering
from right hip and lower back pain since June 12, 2025 after lifting a box of chicken at
work. Diagnoses included unspecified pain in the right hip and lower back. Providers
ordered physical therapy and an MRI of the right hip. Notably, October 1, 2025 was the
first time a WC164 form was completed by a treating provider. PA Bruno assigned work
restrictions of no lifting, repetitive lifting, carrying, or pushing/pulling in excess of 20
pounds. He determined objective findings were consistent with a work-related
mechanism of injury.
11. In a follow-up visit to CareNow Urgent Care on October 22, 2025 Rachel
Ain, MD noted that the original onset date of Claimant’s lower back pain was June 12,
2025. Claimant reported that the injury occurred when he was picking up a box of
chicken. He felt a crack in his lower back/right hip and subsequently experienced pain.
On physical examination, Dr. Ain noted Claimant had an abnormal gait and posture,
right-sided paraspinal tenderness of the lumbar muscles, tenderness over the right hip,
and abnormality of the lower extremity sensation with some decreased sensation along
the right lateral leg. She determined objective findings were consistent with a work-
related mechanism of injury. Dr. Ain assigned work restrictions of no lifting, repetitive
lifting, carrying, or pushing/pulling in excess of 20 pounds. She also recommended an
MRI and six sessions of physical therapy.
12. On December 2, 2025 Claimant returned to Dr. Ain for an examination. Dr.
Ain continued to note that Claimant suffered unspecified pain of the lower back and right

hip. She again remarked that objective findings were consistent with a work-related
mechanism of injury. Dr. Ain continued work restrictions of no lifting, repetitive lifting,
carrying, or pushing/pulling in excess of 20 pounds.
13. On December 15, 2025 Claimant underwent a right hip MRI. The imaging
revealed a localized area of osteonecrosis of the anterosuperior aspect of the right
femoral head with a small tear of the superior aspect of the right acetabular labrum.
14. On December 23, 2025 Dr. Ain explained she was closing Claimant’s case
with CareNow Urgent Care. She noted that “insurance has not approved any treatment
and this led to a significant delay of care.” Dr. Ain remarked that Claimant paid for the
MRI out of pocket, which demonstrated osteonecrosis of the hip. The imaging
corresponded “to where most of his pain is on exam.” Dr. Ain remarked that Claimant
continued to have pain in the lateral spine “and into the hip in that area, and the hip is
his most likely pain generator.” She closed the case because the symptoms were not
work-related. Dr. Ain determined Claimant had reached maximum medical improvement
(MMI) and released him to full duty employment with no permanent impairment.
15. On January 22, 2026 Claimant underwent an independent medical
examination (IME) with John Raschbacher, M.D. Claimant stated to Dr. Raschbacher he
had not been working since August 2025 and denied having a second job. He described
suffering from back or buttock pain on the right side after lifting a box of chicken
weighing 40-50 pounds from the floor to a shelf in a cooler. The reported symptoms
extended to the right foot and toes. After reviewing medical records and diagnostic
imaging, Dr. Raschbacher concluded Claimant suffered from right hip avascular
necrosis (AVN) or osteonecrosis in the right hip. The condition was not caused by lifting,
bending or twisting because AVN is not typically caused by work-related trauma. He
emphasized that “there is simply no work-relatedness with respect to this diagnosis and
his work activities.” Dr. Raschbacher concluded that, because Claimant’s condition was
not related to his work activities, he should be released to regular employment status
with no restrictions or impairment.

16. On March 4, 2026 Qing-Min Chen, MD completed a medical records
review. Dr. Chen agreed with Dr. Raschbacher that Claimant’s hip AVN was not related
to the June 12, 2025 work injury. However, Dr. Chen believed that “this is likely a red
herring.” He remarked that AVN of the hips does not cause numbness or tingling down
the feet. Claimant’s symptoms were more likely related to a nerve injury or some sort of
nerve irritation. Dr. Chen detailed that the hip joint is a deep structure surrounded by a
capsule. Conditions like AVN of the hip and osteoarthritis are not known to cause nerve
irritation going down the leg. He recommended further evaluation, including an MRI of
the lumbar spine. Dr. Chen expected “some sort of disc herniation on the right at L4-L5
or L5-S1 given the distribution of [Claimant’s] symptoms.” He concluded that the original
injury has always been to the lower back and additional treatment might be warranted.
17. Dr. Raschbacher testified at the hearing in this matter. He maintained
Claimant did not suffer a work injury on June 12, 2025. Dr. Raschbacher further
explained that Claimant was diagnosed with AVN or the loss of blood supply to the
femoral head in the hip. AVN is usually an idiopathic condition not caused by any
specific trauma. While any activity, including work, can aggravate the disease, it does
not cause the condition. Moreover, objective findings did not support a compensable
lower back injury. The straight leg raise and tripod sign tests (that indicate a pinched
nerve) were inconsistent. Furthermore, reflex testing was normal and symmetrical.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
1. The purpose of the “Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado” (Act) is to
assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical benefits to injured
workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the necessity of any litigation. §8-
40-102(1), C.R.S. A claimant in a Workers' Compensation claim has the burden of
proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. §8-42-101, C.R.S.
A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-fact, after considering
all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true than not. Page v. Clark, 197
Colo. 306, 592 P.2d 792 (1979); People v. M.A., 104 P.3d 273, 275 (Colo. App. 2004).
The facts in a Workers' Compensation case are not interpreted liberally in favor of either

the rights of the injured worker or the rights of the employer. §8-43-201, C.R.S. A
Workers' Compensation case is decided on its merits. §8-43-201, C.R.S.
2. The Judge’s factual findings concern only evidence that is dispositive of
the issues involved; the Judge has not addressed every piece of evidence that might
lead to a conflicting conclusion and has rejected evidence contrary to the above findings
as unpersuasive. See Magnetic Engineering, Inc. v. ICAO, 5 P.3d 385, 389 (Colo. App.
2000).
3. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness’ testimony and actions; the
reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the testimony and
actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has been contradicted; and
bias, prejudice, or interest. See Prudential Insurance Co. v. Cline, 98 Colo. 275, 57 P.2d
1205 (1936); CJI, Civil 3:16 (2007).
Compensability
4. For a claim to be compensable under the Act, a claimant has the burden of
proving that he suffered a disability that was proximately caused by an injury arising out
of and within the course and scope of employment. §8-41-301(1)(c) C.R.S.; In re
Swanson, W.C. No. 4-589-645 (ICAO, Sept. 13, 2006). Proof of causation is a threshold
requirement that an injured employee must establish by a preponderance of the evidence
before any compensation is awarded. Faulkner v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 12 P.3d 844,
846 (Colo. App. 2000); Singleton v. Kenya Corp., 961 P.2d 571, 574 (Colo. App. 1998).
The question of causation is generally one of fact for determination by the Judge.
Faulkner, 12 P.3d at 846.
5. A pre-existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim
if the employment aggravates, accelerates or combines with the pre-existing condition to
produce a need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d
999, 1001 (Colo. App. 2004). A compensable injury is one that causes disability or the
need for medical treatment. City of Boulder v. Payne, 162 Colo. 345, 426 P.2d 194 (1967);
Mailand v. PSC Indus. Outsourcing LP, W.C. No. 4-898-391-01, (ICAO, Aug. 25, 2014).

6. The mere fact a claimant experiences symptoms while performing work
does not require the inference that there has been an aggravation or acceleration of a
pre-existing condition. See Cotts v. Exempla, Inc., W.C. No. 4-606-563 (ICAO, Aug. 18,
2005). Rather, the symptoms could represent the “logical and recurrent consequence” of
the pre-existing condition. See F.R. Orr Construction v. Rinta, 717 P.2d 965 (Colo. App.
1985); Chasteen v. King Soopers, Inc., W.C. No. 4-445-608 (ICAO, Apr. 10, 2008). As
explained in Scully v. Hooters of Colorado Springs, W.C. No. 4-745-712 (ICAO, Oct. 27,
2008), simply because a claimant’s symptoms arise after the performance of a job
function does not necessarily create a causal relationship based on temporal proximity.
The panel in Scully noted that “correlation is not causation,” and merely because a
coincidental correlation exists between the claimant’s work and symptoms does not mean
there is a causal connection between the claimant’s injury and work activities.
7. Claimant has established it is more probably true than not that he suffered
a compensable lower back injury during the course and scope of employment with
Employer on June 12, 2025. Claimant credibly testified that he experienced immediate
lower back pain on June 12, 2025 while lifting a box of chicken to place it on a shelf in
Employer’s cooler. He believed the pain would resolve and waited to seek professional
medical care in the form of chiropractic treatment on August 18, 2025. He continued to
experience pain that necessitated multiple emergency room visits at Denver Health.
Claimant’s testimony is consistent with the medical records and reflects that he regularly
reported back pain and sciatica on the right side to his providers.
8. After a right hip MRI discovered an AVN condition, Dr. Ain concluded
Claimant’s continuing pain was not related to his reported June 12, 2025 work injury.
She commented that Claimant continued to have pain in the lateral spine “and into the
hip in that area, and the hip is his most likely pain generator.” Similarly, Dr.
Raschbacher reasoned that Claimant’s AVN was not caused by lifting, bending or
twisting because AVN is not typically caused by work-related trauma. He emphasized
that “there is simply no work-relatedness with respect to this diagnosis and his work
activities.” Nevertheless, medical records from treating providers and Dr. Raschbacher’s
IME report consistently document Claimant’s complaints of back pain with right-sided
radiation down the leg.

9. Although Dr. Chen agreed that Claimant’s AVN was unrelated to his work
activities, he reasoned Claimant had sustained a lower back injury on June 12, 2025.
Claimant’s consistent report of pain in the lower back and distribution of symptoms is
consistent with Claimant’s alleged injury. While Claimant may also suffer from a non-
work-related AVN or osteonecrosis condition as documented in the right hip MRI, that
finding is not pertinent to the determination of whether Claimant suffered an injury to his
lower back on June 12, 2025. Notably, Dr. Chen believed that “this is likely a red
herring.” Dr. Chen explained that AVN of the hips does not cause numbness or tingling
down into the feet. Claimant’s symptoms are thus more likely related to a nerve injury or
some sort of nerve irritation. Dr. Chen detailed that the hip joint is a deep structure
surrounded by a capsule. He expected “some sort of disc herniation on the right at L4-
L5 or L5-S1 given the distribution of [Claimant’s] symptoms.” Dr. Chen concluded that
the original injury has always been to the lower back and additional treatment might be
warranted.
10. Dr. Raschbacher’s opinion that Claimant did not sustain a compensable
work injury on June 12, 2025 because the AVN was idiopathic is not persuasive.
Although he acknowledged that Claimant reported back pain with radiation into the leg,
both in the medical records and during the IME, he failed to provide any causation
analysis regarding the lowerback condition in his written report. His conclusions, like
those of Dr. Ain, rested largely on the assumption that Claimant’s righthip condition was
not work related. However, the evidence demonstrates that it is more likely than not that
Claimant’s injury on June 12, 2025 involved the lower back rather than the hip. Dr.
‑
Chen’s opinion aligns with the medical records and Claimant’s testimony. Accordingly,
Claimant’s June 12, 2025 work activities caused, aggravated, accelerated or combined
with his pre-existing lower back condition to produce a need for medical treatment.
Medical Benefits/Right of Selection
11. Respondents are liable for authorized medical treatment that is reasonable
and necessary to cure or relieve the effects of an industrial injury. §8-42101(1)(a),
C.R.S.; Colorado Comp. Ins. Auth. v. Nofio, 886 P.2d 714, 716 (Colo. 1994). A pre-

existing condition or susceptibility to injury does not disqualify a claim if the employment
aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing condition to produce a need
for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 107 P.3d 999, 1001 (Colo.
App. 2004). The question of whether a particular disability is the result of the natural
progression of a pre-existing condition, or the subsequent aggravation or acceleration of
that condition, is itself a question of fact. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 43 P.3d 637 (Colo. App. 2001). Finally, the determination of whether a
particular treatment modality is reasonable and necessary to treat an industrial injury is
a factual determination for the ALJ. In re Parker, W.C. No. 4-517-537 (ICAO, May 31,
2006); In re Frazier, W.C. No. 3-920-202 (ICAO, Nov. 13, 2000).
12. Section 8-41-301(1)(c), C.R.S. requires that an injury be “proximately
caused by an injury or occupational disease arising out of and in the course of the
employee’s employment.” Thus, the claimant is required to prove a direct causal
relationship between the injury and the disability and need for treatment. However, the
industrial injury need not be the sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant,
direct, and consequential factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus.
Claim Appeals Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
13. Section 8-43-404(5)(a), C.R.S. permits an employer or insurer to select the
treating physician in the first instance. Yeck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 996 P.2d, 228,
229 (Colo. App. 1999). However, the Colorado Workers’ Compensation Act requires
respondents to provide injured workers with a list of at least four designated treatment
providers. §8-43-404(5)(a)(I)(A), C.R.S. Specifically, if the employer or insurer fails to
provide an injured worker with a list of at least four physicians or corporate medical
providers, “the employee shall have the right to select a physician.” §8-43-404(5)(a)(I)(A),
C.R.S. W.C.R.P. Rule 8-2 further clarifies that once an employer is on notice that an on-
the-job injury has occurred, “the employer shall provide the injured worker with a written
list of designated providers.” W.C.R.P. Rule 8-2(E) additionally provides that the remedy
for failure to comply with the preceding requirement is that “the injured worker may select
an authorized treating physician of the worker’s choosing.”

14. The term “select,” is unambiguous and should be construed to mean “the
act of making a choice or picking out a preference from among several alternatives.”
Squitieri v. Tayco Screen Printing, Inc., WC 4-421-960 (ICAO Sept. 18, 2000); see In re
Loy, W.C. No. 4-972-625-01 (ICAO, Feb. 19, 2016). Thus, a claimant “selects” a
physician when she “demonstrates by words or conduct that [she] has chosen a
physician to treat the industrial injury.” Williams v. Halliburton Energy Services, WC 4-
995-888-01 (ICAO, Oct. 28, 2016); Loy v. Dillon Companies, W.C. No. 4-972-625 (Feb.
19, 2016). The question of whether the claimant selected a particular physician as the
ATP is one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Squitieri v. Tayco Screen Printing, Inc.,
WC 4-421-960 (ICAO, Sept. 18, 2000).
15. Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that the right to
select an ATP passed to him through Respondents’ failure to provide a written list of at
least four designated medical providers in violation of §8-43-404(5), C.R.S. and WCRP
Rule 8-2. The record reflects that Claimant did not receive a list of at least four
designated medical providers. Respondents have thus not met the requirements of
WCRP 8-2 by tendering a written letter within seven days of the injury. Because
Respondents failed to provide Claimant with a written list of designated providers, the
right to select an ATP passed to him.
16. Claimant has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that he is
entitled to reasonable, necessary and causally related medical benefits for his June 12,
2025 industrial injury. Claimant sought medical treatment and diagnostic imaging on his
own from Aim High Health, LLC, Denver Health, HCA HealthONE, CareNow Urgent
Care, and SimonMed. These providers offered treatment for Claimant’s lower back and
imaging in effort to diagnose his condition. The preceding providers delivered
reasonable, necessary, and related medical care to Claimant. He has thus proven by a
preponderance of the evidence that all of his medical care was authorized, reasonable,
necessary and causally related to his work-related June 12, 2025 lower back injury.
Temporary Partial Disability Benefits

17. Section 8-42-106(1), C.R.S., provides for an award of TPD benefits to be
based on the difference between the claimant’s AWW at the time of injury and the
earnings during the continuance of the temporary partial disability. In order to receive
TPD benefits the claimant must establish the injury caused the disability and
consequent partial wage loss. §8-42-103(1), C.R.S.; see Safeway Stores, Inc. v.
Husson, 732 P.2d 1244 (Colo. App. 1986) (temporary partial compensation benefits are
designed as a partial substitute for lost wages or impaired earning capacity arising from
a compensable injury). When an employee is only partially disabled, TPD benefits are
calculated by determining 66 2/3 of the difference between the employee’s AWW at the
time of the injury and the employee’s AWW during the continuance of the temporary
partial disability. See §8-42-106(1), C.R.S.
18. Claimant has demonstrated by a preponderance of the evidence that he is
entitled to receive TPD benefits for the period July 15, 2025 through August 25, 2025.
Claimant began earning reduced wages as a result of the June 12, 2025 compensable
injury from July 15, 2025 through August 25, 2025, which constitutes a total of six
weeks. Based on the stipulated AWW of $752.40, Claimant would have received
$4,514.40 in gross earnings ($752.40 x 6). However, based on the earnings records in
evidence, Claimant earned a total of $738.30 in wages. Two-thirds of the difference
between $4,514.40 and $738.30 is $2,517.40. Thus, Claimant is entitled to $2,517.40 in
TPD benefits.
Temporary Total Disability Benefits
19. To prove entitlement to TTD benefits a claimant must demonstrate that the
industrial injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he left work as a
result of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss. See §8-42-105,
C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102 P.3d 323 (Colo. 2004); City of Colorado
Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d 637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-
103(1)(a), C.R.S. requires the claimant to establish a causal connection between a
work-related injury and a subsequent wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. The
term “disability” connotes two elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or
restriction of bodily function; and (2) impairment of wage-earning capacity as
demonstrated by claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace

Electric, 971 P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work, or by restrictions that impair
the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her regular employment.
Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo. App. 1998) (citing Ricks v.
Indus. Claim Appeals Off., P.2d 1118 (Colo. App. 1991)). Because there is no
requirement that a claimant must produce evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s
testimony alone is sufficient to demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952
P.2d 831, 833 (Colo. App. 1997). TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence
of any of the following: (1) the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to
regular or modified employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a
written release to return to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the
employee a written release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered
in writing and the employee fails to begin the employment. §8-42-105(3)(a)-(d), C.R.S.
20. Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that he is
entitled to receive TTD benefits from August 26, 2025 until terminated by statute.
Claimant’s credible testimony demonstrates that he was terminated from his
employment as of August 25, 2025 due to his inability to complete a full workday or
perform his prior work with Employer because of his back injury. Claimant’s testimony
was further supported by the imposition of work restrictions beginning on October 1,
2025 when the WC164 form was first completed. Based on an AWW of $752.40,
Claimant’s TTD rate is $501.60. Respondents thus owe TTD benefits beginning August
26, 2025 and continuing until terminated by statute at the rate of $501.60.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant suffered a compensable lower back injury while working for
Employer on June 12, 2025.
2. The right to select an ATP has passed to Claimant. Claimant shall notify
Respondents of his ATP choice within 20 days of the date this order is served.
3. Claimant is entitled to reasonable and necessary medical benefits related
to his June 12, 2025 work injury. Claimant’s treatment at Aim High Health, LLC, Denver

Health, HCA HealthONE, CareNow Urgent Care, and SimonMed was reasonable,
necessary, and related to his June 12, 2025 work injury. Respondents shall pay for the
associated costs of the treatment, as well as other reasonable, necessary and related
medical care.
4. Claimant earned an AWW of $752.40.
5. Claimant is entitled to receive TPD benefits from July 15, 2025 through
August 25, 2025. Respondents shall pay Claimant total TPD benefits of $2,517.40.
6. Respondents shall pay Claimant TTD benefits at a rate of $501.60
beginning August 26, 2025 and continuing until terminated by statute.
7. Respondents shall pay statutory interest at a rate of 8% per annum on
compensation benefits not paid when due.
8. Any issues not resolved in this Order are reserved for future
determination.
If you are dissatisfied with the Judge's order, you may file a Petition to Review
the order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the Judge's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the Judge; and (2) That
you mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. For
statutory reference, see section 8-43-301(2), C.R.S. For further information regarding
procedures to follow when filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may
access a petition to review form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
